en: Admonition for Beginners in Study:
A person who is a beginner must distance themselves from evil friends and draw near to the virtuous and good.

Having received the five precepts, the ten precepts, and so forth, they should properly understand what is to be observed and what is to be transgressed, as well as the permissions and prohibitions. They should rely solely upon the holy words spoken by the Golden Mouth [the Buddha] and not follow [other teachers].
Those of common and deluded speech,
having already left the household life to join the ranks of the pure assembly,
should constantly maintain gentleness, kindness, and compliance, and must not harbor arrogance or pride.
The elder shall be the elder brother and the younger the younger brother.
Should any disputes arise, they shall be reconciled through two-fold counsel;
they shall simply direct their hearts toward one another with loving-kindness.
One must not use harsh speech to wound others.
If one treats one's companions with contempt or engages in idle gossip about right and wrong,
such an act of renunciation is entirely devoid of benefit.

The calamity of wealth and sensual desire is more severe than that of a venomous snake; one should examine oneself and recognize the impermanence [of these things], and must distance oneself from them.
Unless there is a necessary reason, one must not enter the rooms or courtyards of others.
In private places, one must not forcibly pry into the affairs of others.
One must not wash one's undergarments for six days.
When performing ablutions or rinsing the mouth, one must not make loud noises, nor spit or blow one's nose.
When taking turns to offer incense, one must not jostle others or disrupt the proper order.
While walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), one must not expose the chest or swing the arms.
While engaged in conversation, one must not speak loudly or laugh in jest.
Unless there is an essential matter, one must not go outside the gate.
One must protect the sick with a compassionate heart;
upon seeing guests, one must receive them with joy;
and when encountering elders or superiors, one must show solemn respect and yield the way.
In preparing ritual implements, one must be frugal and practice contentment.
When eating the vegetarian meal, one must not make noise while drinking or sipping;
one must remain composed and steady, neither lifting the face nor looking around.
One must not harbor feelings of attachment toward the refined or aversion toward the coarse;
one must remain silent and refrain from speech,
and must guard against discursive thoughts.
One must understand that receiving food is solely for the purpose of curing the withered body so as to accomplish the work of the Way.
One must contemplate the Heart Sutra of Prajñāpāramitā, observing the purity of the three wheels, so as not to contravene the application of the Way.
When attending to ritual cultivation, one must practice diligently at both dawn and dusk, esteeming oneself and avoiding indolence.
One must know the sequence of the various practices so as not to allow confusion.
When chanting praises and offering prayers of blessing, one must recite the text while contemplating its meaning;
one must not merely follow the sounds of the voice.
One must not allow the chanting to become melodic or discordant.
In gazing with reverence upon the Honored Countenance, one must not let the mind wander toward external objects.
One must recognize that one's own karmic obstacles are as vast as mountains and oceans.
One should know that both ritual repentance (*sī-chàn*) and factual repentance (*shì-chàn*) can eliminate transgressions.
One should deeply contemplate that both the one who prostrates and the object of prostration arise through dependent origination from true nature (*tathatā*).
One should have deep faith that response and resonance are not in vain, for cause and effect follow one another.
When residing in the communal quarters, one must yield to others and not contend;
one must mutually support and protect one another,
and be careful and deliberate in discussing matters of victory or defeat.
Be careful not to engage in idle chatter while gathered together.
Be careful not to put on another's shoes by mistake.
Be careful not to sit or lie down out of order.
When conversing with visitors, one must not air the family’s private failings;
rather, one should only praise the temple’s affairs and Buddhist services.
One must not visit the storehouse to witness or hear miscellaneous matters that might give rise to doubt.
Unless there is a matter of necessity, one must not travel through prefectures or hunt in counties,
nor engage with worldly people in ways that cause others to harbor resentment and jealousy, thereby losing the spirit of one's own Way.
Should there be a matter of necessity requiring one to go abroad, [one must act with restraint].
Inform the abbot and the administrators of the community so that they may know your destination.
If you enter a layperson’s home, you must resolutely maintain right mindfulness.
Be careful not to allow your minds to wander into depravity upon seeing forms or hearing sounds.
How much more so should you refrain from loosening your robes to laugh and jest, engaging in idle chatter about miscellaneous matters,
consuming food or drink at improper times, or recklessly performing acts that claim to be free of hindrance— all of which deeply contravene the Buddha’s precepts.
Furthermore, to dwell amidst the suspicions of virtuous and good people—
how could one be considered a person of wisdom?
He resided at the shrine hall and lived in careful association with novice monks.
Be cautious in social interactions.
Be cautious in observing the likes and dislikes of others.
Be cautious in greedily seeking out written texts.
Be careful not to oversleep; be careful not to allow the mind to scatter and pursue external objects.
If you encounter a teacher ascending the seat to preach the Dharma, [be attentive].
By all means, you must not conceive of the Dharma as being like a precipice and give rise to a mind of despondency,
nor should you conceive of it as something you have heard repeatedly and develop a sense of ease;
you must listen with an open and humble heart.
There must inevitably come a time when the trigger is pulled;
one must not merely follow those who parrot the words and take only their verbal proficiency as the goal—
what is called "a snake drinking water that turns to poison."
When a cow drinks water, it becomes milk;
when the wise study, they achieve Bodhi;
when the foolish study, they achieve birth and death—this is the principle.
Furthermore, one must not harbor thoughts of contempt for the Master of the Dharma;
doing so creates obstacles on the Path and prevents further progress, so one must be most careful.
The treatise says:
It is like a person traveling at night who encounters a criminal holding a torch across the road;
if one refuses the light because of the person's wickedness, [one is at fault].
One has fallen into a pit and tumbled down a trench;
having heard the Dharma, one proceeds as if treading upon thin ice.
One must necessarily strain the ears and eyes to listen to the profound sound.
Restraining the dust of worldly passions, he appreciated its profound elegance;
after descending from the hall, he sat in silence to contemplate it,
and as if harboring some doubt, he extensively questioned those who were awakened to the truth.
Being vigilant at evening and seeking counsel at dawn, one errs not by even a hair’s breadth.
Only in this way can right faith arise;
such is the mark of one who holds the Way in their heart.
The mind-ground has been habituated since beginningless time to the entanglements of craving, hatred, and delusion;
though these may be temporarily suppressed, they arise again like a tertian malaria.
At all times, one must directly employ the power of applied effort, skillful means, and wisdom to protect oneself with great diligence.
How could one idly engage in frivolous talk and vainly waste the days of heaven without foundation,
hoping thereby to seek the heart-essence and find a way out? Rather, one should simply firm up one's resolve,
hold fast to one's integrity, and scrutinize oneself with unwearied diligence.
Knowing what is not right, one reforms and repents, becoming supple and harmonious;
through diligent cultivation, the power of contemplation deepens,
and through refinement and polishing, the gateway of practice becomes increasingly pure.
Constantly maintaining the thought that [the Dharma] is difficult to encounter, one’s path-practice remains ever fresh;
always harboring a heart of joy and fortune, one never regresses.
Thus, after a long time, concentration and wisdom naturally become perfectly clear and bright, and one perceives the nature of one's own mind.
Employing wisdom and compassion that are like illusions, you shall again deliver sentient beings and become a great field of merit for humans and devas;
you must exert yourselves with all diligence.

First, he asked himself,
"Do you believe this? and the Mountain replied:
"If your faith is not sufficient, you will not reach this point.
The Master said,
"Even if you have full confidence, you must further maintain the precepts."
"Maintaining the precepts is easy to achieve spiritual efficacy.
If one lacks the practice of the precepts, it is like building a multi-storied pavilion in mid-air.
Mañjuśrī asked, "Do you still maintain the precepts? Mazu said: [He remained silent].
Seeing that he was observing the five precepts,
the Master said,
"From this point forward, simply look at this word 'Mu' (無)."
Do not engage in conceptual deliberation or intellectual speculation.
Do not attempt to understand through the lens of existence or non-existence.
Furthermore, do not look at scriptures, commentaries, or recorded sayings.
Simply hold up the word "Mu" alone.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day and within the four modes of deportment,
you must remain alert and mindful— like a cat stalking a mouse or a hen brooding over her eggs— without allowing it to be interrupted.
When you have not yet attained thorough penetration,
it will be as unalterable as a rat gnawing at a coffin.
At such times, repeatedly whip up the clouds of doubt.
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. Why did Zhaozhou say "no"?
If you have doubts, silently hold fast to the word "no," turn the light inward, and look for yourself.
One must recognize this very "no-word" to know oneself;
to know Zhaozhou; and to capture the point where the Buddhas and Patriarchs are despised by others.
Simply believe these words of mine and proceed directly;
there will certainly come a time of awakening.

Regarding the *Dharma Words for Sending a Disciple on a Pilgrimage* by Master Dongshan Chong: "In general, one who travels on pilgrimage must take this Way as their primary concern."
One must not accept offerings as they arise and pass the days in negligence; rather,
one must nail the two characters "birth-and-death" (saṃsāra) upon the forehead and,
throughout the twelve periods of the day, tear open the skin of one's face.
You must investigate until you reach a clear understanding;
otherwise, if you merely follow the crowd and pass your time in vain,
the Old Man Yama will settle your bill for the meals when the time comes.
Do not say that I do not speak to you.
If you are to apply yourself to practice, you must calculate it day by day and examine yourself moment by moment.
Observe from when you rise from your mat until the second watch of the night.
Where is it that one fails to gain power?
Where is it that one loses the mark?
Where is it that one does not lose the mark?
If you proceed in this manner,
there will certainly come a time when you reach your destination.
There are some who endeavor in the Way who neither read the sutras nor pay homage to the Buddha.
As soon as one ascends the meditation seat, one immediately falls into a daze;
by the time one awakens, one is again lost in idle and confused thoughts.
As soon as one descends from the meditation seat, one immediately engages in worldly entanglements with others.
If you practice the Way in this manner until the time of Maitreya’s descent,
you will still not have reached the point of entry.
You must rouse your spirit with fierce intensity and bring forth the single word "Wu" (No).
Three times by day and three times by night, you must engage with others;
you must not remain sitting idly in a state of armor-like stillness,
nor must you cling to sitting rigidly upon a meditation cushion.
One must keep it alive and active.
When myriad discursive thoughts arise in profusion, one must by no means engage them in combat;
for the more one fights with them, the more frantic they become.
Many people here do not recognize when to advance or retreat, nor how to find release;
they become wind-blown and dazed, ruining their entire lives.

like when a ladle of cold water is added to a pot of hot soup.

If your practice has not yet gained entry,
do not give rise to affliction.
Fearing that the demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*) might enter the mind,
if one perceives a reduction in effort, one must not give rise to joy;
fearing that the demon of joy (*prāmodyamāra*) might enter the mind.

Abandoning the conditions of this world, removing attachment and inverted views,
take the reality of birth and death as your great matter;
be willing to comply with the regulations of the hermitage.
Sever ties with worldly affairs and enjoy things as they come.
Except for the three periods of the night, do not permit sleep;
do not permit going out into the streets.
One is not permitted to attend invitations;
one has not yet been granted permission to engage in study or recitation;
and one is not permitted to read the scriptures unless invited by an official authority.
If, after three years of diligent practice according to the Dharma,
you still do not see your nature and penetrate the source,

Postscript: Now, as for the mind, it is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane.
All phenomena are the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the mind.
However, there are five distinct types.
The first is the "flesh-ball mind," which is shaped like a plantain bud.
First, the physical body born within the realm of form,
which is categorized as insentient matter;
second, the mind that engages in cognitive reflection.
It resembles a wild fire,
appearing and vanishing suddenly;
it is categorized as a product of deluded thought.
The third is the mind that gathers and initiates [existence],
which resembles a seed of grass;
it lies in ambush within the field of consciousness.
It is comprised of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The fourth, the ālayavijñāna,
is like a fertile field.
The planting of seeds is insatiable;
it is subsumed under ignorance.
These are the five aspects of the mind of true suchness.
Its form is identical to empty space;
it is vast and penetrating throughout the Dharma-realm,
encompassing both quiescence and illumination.
Regarding the five states of mind mentioned above,
the first four are all delusory thoughts that arise and perish moment by moment; the last one is the true state,
which is uniform throughout the three periods of time.
If one does not discern and distinguish with clarity,
there remains the fear that the false will be mistaken for the true;
such an error is no small matter.
Therefore, I cite the scriptures of the Buddha and the words of the patriarchs to interrogate,
debate, examine, and explain,
thereby revealing the source of delusion and ignorance.
This work details the beginning and end of cultivation and realization in sixteen successive chapters,
commencing with right faith.
Bringing the journey to its ultimate conclusion,
it provides a profound clarification of the shortcut to the true mind;
therefore, it is titled "Direct Exposition."
